core_idea: Classify each pile only by the position of its least significant set bit. The minimum such position determines whether a player can force the game into a uniform lower layer, while even-minimum mixed states can be maintained forever, leading to a draw.
key_observations: A terminal state is exactly when every pile has least significant bit position 0, because all piles are odd.
If all piles have the same least significant bit position c > 0, any move decreases every pile's position to c - 1.
Choosing a pile whose least significant bit equals the current minimum makes all piles collapse to one common lower position.
The parity of the minimum least-significant-bit position determines whether collapsing the state gives the opponent a losing or winning layer.
When the minimum is even but not all piles attain it, players can avoid collapse by repeatedly choosing a pile above the minimum, preserving a mixed state and forcing a draw.
Counting configurations can be done by fixing the exact minimum least-significant-bit position, using counts of numbers divisible by powers of two.
reasoning_patterns: Replace large numeric states with a small invariant that fully controls game behavior.
Analyze game moves through monotone layers of an invariant rather than raw values.
Classify impartial game outcomes by identifying forced transitions between canonical state classes.
Separate decisive states from indefinitely maintainable states to account for draws.
Count objects by fixing the exact minimum value of a statistic.
Use cumulative counts and subtraction to count exact-value classes.
